title: BGP/MPLS VPNs
summary: Describes a method by which a service provider with an IP backbone can offer VPNs to its customers, using BGP to distribute routes and MPLS to forward packets. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 4364.

eli5.summary: A big network company can let many customers share the same wires while each customer sees only their own private network.

questions: how do service providers build vpns with bgp and mpls
what is a bgp mpls vpn
subtitle: How a service provider can run many customers' private IP networks over one shared backbone, using BGP for routes and MPLS for forwarding.

tldr.problem: A service provider wants to sell private IP networks (VPNs) to many customers over one shared backbone, even when customers reuse the same addresses, without every backbone router having to hold every customer's routes.
tldr.mechanism: Provider edge routers keep a separate forwarding table per customer site, turn customer prefixes into 12-byte VPN-IPv4 addresses, share them with BGP, and carry packets across the backbone with a two-level MPLS label stack.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 4364, which is the current specification of the method.

today: RFC 2547 is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 4364, which now describes BGP/MPLS IP VPNs.

sections.title: Virtual Private Networks and Their Goals
sections.content:
RFC 2547 describes how a Service Provider (SP) with an IP backbone can offer Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) to its customers. A VPN is a set of customer sites that may talk to each other over the backbone; two sites with no VPN in common have no connectivity. MPLS is used to forward packets over the backbone and BGP is used to distribute routes.

The main goal is to let an enterprise outsource its IP backbone in a way that is simple for the enterprise and still scalable for the provider. The memo is not aimed at VPNs over the public Internet.

The model sets out several properties. VPNs with no sites in common may use overlapping address spaces. A site in several VPNs may need different routes to the same system, for example sending extranet traffic through a firewall but not intranet traffic. Routing information for a VPN should live only in the routers attached to that VPN, and the security should be equivalent to a level 2 backbone such as Frame Relay.
sections.eli5: Imagine one big road system shared by many companies, where each company's cars can only drive to that company's own buildings. The companies can even reuse the same street names without getting mixed up.

sections.title: Sites, CE Devices and PE Routers
sections.content:
At each site, one or more Customer Edge (CE) devices connect over some data link (PPP, ATM, Ethernet, Frame Relay, a GRE tunnel and so on) to one or more Provider Edge (PE) routers. A CE is usually a router. It is a routing peer of its PE, but not of CE routers at other sites, so very large VPNs are easy to support. The backbone also contains P routers, which do not attach to CE devices.

A site is a set of IP systems that can reach each other without using the backbone. A CE belongs to one site, a site may be in many VPNs, and a PE may attach to CEs in any number of sites. The PE and P routers are administered only by the SP, and the CE devices only by the customer, unless that management is contracted out.

Each PE keeps one or more per-site forwarding tables. A packet's destination is looked up in a table only if the packet arrived directly from a site tied to that table. A table holds only routes to sites that share at least one VPN with that site. If there is no match, the packet is discarded, unless the SP provides Internet access for the site, in which case the PE's Internet table is consulted.

A customer can also split a site into virtual sites, for example by VLANs or sub-interfaces, each with its own set of VPNs and its own forwarding table in the PE.
sections.eli5: Each office has a front door guard (the PE) with a private address book. The guard only lists offices that office is allowed to visit, so a package can never be sent to the wrong company.

sections.title: VPN-IPv4 Addresses and Route Distribution
sections.content:
BGP normally keeps only one route per address prefix, but different VPNs may reuse the same prefix. RFC 2547 solves this with a new BGP address family, VPN-IPv4, carried using the BGP Multiprotocol Extensions (RFC 2283).

A VPN-IPv4 address is a 12-byte quantity: an 8-byte Route Distinguisher (RD) followed by a 4-byte IPv4 address. The RD makes identical IPv4 prefixes in different VPNs unique, so BGP can hold a separate route for each. The RD adds no meaning of its own and says nothing about which VPNs a route goes to. It can also be used to create several different routes to the very same system.

An RD has a two-byte type field, an administrator field and an assigned number field. For example, the administrator field can hold an Autonomous System number and the 4-byte number field a value assigned by that provider. This lets each SP manage its own numbering space. When BGP compares prefixes it ignores this structure. When a packet is matched against a VPN-IPv4 route, only the IPv4 part is matched.

Which sites get which routes is controlled by attributes carried in BGP. Every per-site forwarding table is associated with one or more Target VPN attributes, and every VPN-IPv4 route is created with one or more of them. A route with Target VPN T must go to every PE that has a table associated with T, where it is eligible to be installed. A route has one RD but may have several Target VPNs, which scales better than creating more routes. The memo notes that this attribute could more accurately be called a "Route Target".

A route may also carry a VPN of Origin attribute, which identifies the set of sites it came from. Together the two attributes build different shapes: a Closed User Group uses one Target value for all its sites, and a hub and spoke VPN uses one value for "Hub" and one for "Spoke".

PEs in one Autonomous System exchange routes over IBGP, directly or via a route reflector. Across Autonomous Systems, routes pass through ASBRs using EBGP, but only at private peering points under a trusted arrangement. VPN-IPv4 routes must not be distributed to or accepted from the public Internet. A PE uses its own address as BGP next hop and also distributes an MPLS label with the route. A PE must filter out routes for VPNs it is not attached to, and a P router never installs VPN-IPv4 routes.
sections.eli5:
Two schools might both have a room called 'Room 5'. Putting the school's name in front makes each one different, so the mail carrier never mixes them up.

Each route gets coloured stickers saying which groups may see it. A router only keeps the routes with stickers for groups it belongs to.

sections.title: Forwarding Across the Backbone
sections.content:
Packets cross the backbone using MPLS with a two-level label stack. PE routers (and ASBRs that redistribute VPN-IPv4 routes) put /32 prefixes for themselves into the backbone IGP, so MPLS can assign labels toward each PE.

When a PE receives a packet from a CE, it looks up the destination in the right per-site table. If the destination is on the same PE, it sends the packet straight to that CE. Otherwise it pushes the label that the BGP next hop assigned for that destination as the bottom label. Then it pushes the label for the IGP next hop toward the BGP next hop as the top label, and forwards the packet. If the two next hops are the same, the second label may not be needed.

From then on every decision is made by MPLS and the IP header is not examined until the packet reaches the CE. The last PE pops the final label, so the CE sees an ordinary IP packet. The two labels keep all VPN routes out of the P routers, which is crucial for scalability.
sections.eli5: A parcel gets two stickers. The outer sticker tells the middle sorting centres how to reach the right exit building, and the inner sticker tells that building which customer it is for.

sections.title: Learning Routes Between PE and CE
sections.content:
A PE learns a site's routes from its CE and converts them to VPN-IPv4 routes using a configured RD. Site routes are never leaked into the backbone IGP. The memo lists the ways a PE and CE can exchange routes: static routing, RIP, OSPF, or BGP. Static routing and OSPF are for stub VPNs only. A transit VPN receives routes from a third party and passes them to a PE, while most VPNs, including nearly all corporate networks, are expected to be stubs.

The memo calls BGP between PE and CE by far the best technique technically. It avoids running several routing algorithm instances on the PE, it is designed to pass routes between administrations, it copes with BGP backdoors, and it lets the CE suggest a Target per route. Its drawback is that CE administrators may find BGP new.

Before redistributing a learned route, the PE assigns three attributes: Site of Origin, VPN of Origin and Target VPN. A route whose Site of Origin names a site must never be sent to a CE at that site, which prevents loops. In the other direction, a PE may send a CE any route in that site's table, though often just a default route is enough. If the CE supports MPLS, the PE can give it a label per route.
sections.eli5: Each office tells its guard which addresses are inside it, and the guard translates them into the provider's special long addresses. The guard also tells the office how to reach the rest, or just says 'send everything to me'.

sections.title: Security, QoS and Scalability
sections.content:
The memo says the security is virtually identical to that of Frame Relay or ATM VPNs, provided two conditions hold. Backbone routers must not accept labeled packets from untrusted sources unless the packets leave the backbone before the IP header or lower labels are inspected, and labeled VPN-IPv4 routes must not be accepted from untrusted sources. It argues that MPLS makes this simpler than IP-within-IP tunnelling. Customers wanting more can add IPsec Tunnel Mode, and the memo discusses pairwise tunnels between CE routers and a shared multi-party security association. The formal Security Considerations section only says that security issues are discussed throughout the memo.

For quality of service, existing L3 QoS can be applied to labeled packets using the experimental bits in the shim header, and traffic engineering applies directly.

On scalability, P routers hold no VPN routes. A PE holds routes only for VPNs it attaches to, and route reflectors and ASBRs can be partitioned among VPNs. So no single component holds all routes and capacity is not limited by any one device.
sections.eli5: The system stays safe as long as the provider only lets trusted parties hand it packets and routes. It also stays fast because no single box has to remember everyone's addresses.
